summary: This note covers the goodwill greetings used during the Christmas and holiday season, which vary by culture and location. Traditional greetings such as "Merry Christmas," "Happy Christmas," and "Happy New Year" were long predominant, while more generic greetings like "Happy Holidays" and "Season's Greetings" rose in prominence in the mid-to-late 20th century United States and later spread to other Western countries. Polls from 2012 show Americans and Canadians still largely preferred "Merry Christmas."
one_line: Overview of traditional versus generic holiday greetings during the Christmas season and recent US and Canadian polling on their use.
key_facts: Traditionally, the predominant greetings of the Christmas season were "Merry Christmas," "Happy Christmas," and "Happy New Year."
In the mid-to-late 20th century in the United States, generic greetings such as "Happy Holidays" and "Season's Greetings" began to rise in cultural prominence.
The use of generic holiday greetings later spread to other Western countries including Canada, Australia, and to a lesser extent some European countries.
The choice of seasonal greeting depends on culture and location, with some greetings more prevalent than others.
A 2012 poll by Rasmussen Reports indicated that 68% of Americans prefer the use of "Merry Christmas."
In the same 2012 Rasmussen Reports poll, 23% of Americans preferred "Happy Holidays."
A similarly timed Canadian poll conducted by Ipsos-Reid indicated that 72% of Canadians preferred "Merry Christmas."
Goodwill greetings during the season are used to address strangers, family, colleagues, or friends.
